paragraph.text: B17. "Animals don't mind, they even like it and, in a way, they consent"

an animal seeming calm doesn't mean they don't mind, and liking affection or food doesn't mean liking being confined, separated from their young or killed. Animals have preferences, and animal welfare science measures how hard they work to get or avoid something. Consent requires understanding and the ability to refuse; animals don't understand what will be done to them, and when they show refusal, by fleeing, resisting or calling for their young, the refusal is ignored. And even an animal who noticed nothing would lose the rest of their life.
"The cow doesn't mind being milked; she even likes it. The hen lays the egg and forgets about it. If they didn't want it, they'd run away."
In the routine of farms, many animals show no obvious signs of suffering.
Some seem to enjoy contact with people and approach of their own accord.
What doesn't bother an animal doesn't harm them, and what they accept without resisting is, in a way, consented to.
So using these animals doesn't harm them.

P1 is only partly true, and it picks the calm moments. P2 is true of certain kinds of contact, such as food and affection, but not of everything that happens to the animal. P3 is false: there are harms the animal doesn't notice at the time, such as death, and accepting without resisting isn't consenting when one doesn't understand what will happen and can't refuse.
: P3 confuses not reacting with not being harmed, and calm with consent.
"The hen lays the egg and forgets about it."
"If they didn't want it, they'd run away."
"The pig comes running when he sees me; he likes it."
"The fish took the bait because it wanted to."
"Horses like working and being ridden." (which is I22)

A dog can like getting a treat and still not like being locked up. It's the same with farm animals: the cow may like grass and being petted, but she calls for her calf when he is taken away. Liking one thing doesn't mean liking everything.

Seeming calm isn't the same as not minding, and liking food or affection isn't liking being confined, separated from one's young or killed. Cows separated from their calves call for them and become agitated, and hens work to get a nest to lay in. Consent requires understanding what will happen and being able to refuse; when an animal refuses, by fleeing or resisting, no one respects it. And even if they noticed nothing, they would lose the rest of their life.
"If the animal could refuse, do you think they would agree to go to the slaughterhouse?"
Many moments of the routine are quiet
Separation, confinement, mutilations, transport and slaughter
Food and contact can be good for them
That this says nothing about what comes next
Many were bred to be docile
That docility isn't consent, and that resistance, when it happens, is restrained

text.bold: 1. Animals have preferences, and they can be measured.

paragraph.text: Animal welfare science has developed tests, such as those of the zoologist Marian Dawkins, that measure how hard an animal will work to get access to something or to avoid it. They show that hens, pigs and cows have clear preferences about space, nests, companionship and environment. "Doesn't mind" is an assumption, not an observation.

text.bold: 2. There are clear signs that they care.

paragraph.text: In a study by Daniel Weary and Belinda Chua, published in 2000, cows and calves separated after birth vocalized and became agitated, and the reaction was stronger the longer they had been together. Prey species, such as cattle and sheep, also tend to hide signs of pain, which makes suffering seem smaller than it is.

text.bold: 3. Liking a part isn't liking the whole.

paragraph.text: A pig who runs to whoever brings food likes the food, not the truck that will come later. The argument uses the pleasant moments to answer for the others.

text.bold: 4. Consent requires understanding and being able to refuse.

paragraph.text: No animal understands that they will be slaughtered, and none can effectively refuse. In animal research, some argue for respecting at least the animal's refusal, their dissent, as is done with young children. In farming, when an animal resists, the refusal is restrained with fences, chutes and electric prods.

text.bold: 5. Not noticing isn't not being harmed.

paragraph.text: Even if an animal never suffered at any moment, death would take the rest of their life from them. It is a harm of deprivation, which doesn't depend on their noticing it (see B2).
Proposes measuring animals' needs by how hard they work to obtain something, as if paying a price
Basis of the preference and motivation tests used in welfare science

(d) The strongest counter-reply: domesticated animals were bred to be docile, so they suffer little
The most serious version says: thousands of years of domestication produced calm animals, less stressed by human presence. If they really are less bothered, the argument would have a grain of truth.

The principle being tested is: "if someone doesn't resist or seems calm, they aren't harmed, and in a way they consent".
A baby who smiles at a stranger

One's own dog wagging their tail

It's right that many animals have quiet moments, that some enjoy human contact and that domestication produced more docile animals. It's also right to give weight to what the animal feels: that's the right criterion.
But, applied carefully, that criterion turns against the argument: animals have preferences, show when they don't want something and lose their lives at slaughter, whether they notice or not.
